t.5.45.1: But the king, seeing the five generals slain by Hanumān together with their followers and their mounts, turned his gaze upon Prince Akṣa, still unscathed, fierce in battle and eager for the fight.
t.5.45.2: Then he, the valiant one with a bow brightly adorned with gold, urged on by the glance cast upon him by that lord, sprang up in the assembly like a fire in the sacrificial hall roused by an oblation from the foremost of the twice-born.
t.5.45.3: Then that valiant bull among the Nairṛtas mounted a great chariot, radiant as the newly risen sun and covered all over with a network of refined gold, and set out against that mighty monkey.
t.5.45.4: Then the chariot, won through a great store of accumulated austerities, gleaming with a lattice of refined gold, hung with pennants, its standard adorned with jewels, and well yoked with eight excellent horses swift as thought
t.5.45.5: A chariot unassailable by gods and asuras, moving without hindrance, radiant as the sun, coursing through the sky and well equipped, furnished with quivers, handsomely fitted with eight swords, with spears and lances set in their proper order.
t.5.45.7: Filling the sky and the earth with its mountains with the din of horses, elephants and great chariots, he, accompanied by his assembled forces, approached the mighty monkey who was seated, stationed upon the gateway arch.
t.5.45.6: Then he, whose valour equalled that of the immortals, mounted a chariot bright as the sun, resplendent with its full store of equipment, its golden garlands, and a radiance like that of the moon and the sun, and set forth.
t.5.45.8: Having approached that monkey, who stood there like the fire of Time at the end of the age when all creatures perish, the tawny-eyed Akṣa, seized with wonder and agitation, gazed at him with eyes full of deep respect.
t.5.45.9: The mighty son of the king, considering the speed of that great-souled monkey, his valour against his enemies, the sky, and his own strength, grew in power like the sun at the close of winter.
t.5.45.10: Seeing that irresistible prowess, he grew enraged. Standing firm in the fight with a composed mind, he assailed Hanumān in battle with three sharp arrows.
t.5.45.12: He, adorned with golden necklace, armlets and lovely earrings, swift in valour, approached the monkey. The encounter of those two was matchless, causing alarm even to the gods and asuras.
t.5.45.11: Then Akṣa, his spirit roused, arrows in hand and bow firmly grasped, looked closely at that monkey, who was proud, untouched by fatigue, and grown mighty through the defeat of his foes.
t.5.45.13: Beholding the combat between the monkey and the prince, the earth cried out, the sun shone no more, the wind ceased to blow, and the mountain trembled; the sky roared and the ocean was churned into turmoil.
t.5.45.14: Then that hero, who knew the true art of aiming, fitting and releasing arrows, let fall upon the monkey's head three well-pointed, feathered arrows with golden nocks, like venomous serpents.
t.5.45.15: Struck on the head by those arrows all at once, bleeding, his rolling eyes smeared with blood, he looked like the newly risen sun; with the arrows for his rays, he shone like the sun garlanded with beams.
t.5.45.17: Then he, his fury swelling, endowed with strength and valour, like the garlanded sun standing upon the summit of Mandara, burned Prince Akṣa together with his army and his mounts with the fiery rays of his eyes.
t.5.45.16: Then that foremost of the ministers of the lord of the tawny monkeys, beholding in battle that son of the best of kings, bearing splendid lofty weapons and a wondrous bow, rejoiced, and, eager for the fight, he swelled with vigor.
t.5.45.18: Then that rākṣasa-cloud in battle, whose bow was the rainbow and whose downpour was arrows, swiftly released his arrows upon that mountain, the lord of monkeys, as a rain-cloud pours its rain upon the greatest of mountains.
t.5.45.19: Then the monkey, whose prowess was like that of a thundercloud, having beheld in battle the prince Akṣa, fierce in his valor in combat, whose arrows were charged with ever-growing splendor, strength and might, roared with joy.
t.5.45.20: He, made proud of his valor in battle by his youthfulness, his fury swelling and his eyes like blood, rushed in the fight upon the matchless monkey, as an elephant approaches a great pit covered over with grass.
t.5.45.22: That mighty and valorous chief of the rākṣasas, a chariot-warrior most excellent among chariot-fighters, rushed at him as he flew upward, showering him with arrows as a rain-cloud pelts a mountain with showers of stones.
t.5.45.21: Struck by the arrows he had forcefully loosed, he let out a roar, his voice like the rumbling of a thundercloud; and Māruti swiftly sprang up into the sky, dreadful to behold as he flung out his arms and thighs.
t.5.45.24: The son of Māruta gazed with an eye of great esteem upon Akṣa, who had taken up his bow, his face turned toward battle, covering the sky with excellent arrows of many kinds, and he fell into deep thought.
t.5.45.23: That heroic monkey, evading those arrows of his, ranged along the path frequented by the wind; swift as thought and fierce in valour in battle, he darted like the wind through the gaps between the arrows.
t.5.45.25: Then the mighty-armed monkey, his chest pierced with arrows by that great-souled best of princes, roared, and, knowing well the true nature of each particular deed, considered what valour to show in the battle.
t.5.45.26: Radiant as the newly risen sun, this mighty one performs great deeds, not like a boy; and my mind is not inclined here toward slaying him, who shines in every feat of battle.
t.5.45.27: This high-souled one is great in valour, composed, and exceedingly enduring in battle; without doubt, owing to the excellence of his deeds and virtues, he is honoured by the Nāgas and Yakṣas together with the sages.
t.5.45.28: With a mind swelling with valour and zeal, he has come before me and stands there, gazing at me. Indeed, the valour of this swift-acting one could shake the minds even of the suras and asuras.
t.5.45.29: If he is left unchecked, he will surely not fail to overpower us, for his valour only grows in battle. Killing him is what pleases me; a growing fire is not something one can afford to ignore.
t.5.45.30: Thus gauging the onslaught of his foe and planning his own course of action, the valiant and mighty one then gathered his speed, and the great monkey set his mind on slaying him.
t.5.45.31: Then that heroic monkey, the son of the Wind, struck down with blows of his palm, on the wind-frequented path of the sky, those eight horses of his, exceedingly swift, well-trained, and able to bear the load while wheeling about.
t.5.45.33: Abandoning that chariot, the great chariot-warrior, bow in hand and bearing his sword, flew up into the sky, just as a sage of fierce power, through the force of his austerities, casting off his body, rises to the abode of the Maruts.
t.5.45.32: Then that great chariot-warrior, struck by the palm of his hand and vanquished by the minister of the lord of the tawny ones, fell from the sky to the ground, the seat of his chariot shattered, its pole wrenched loose and his horses slain.
t.5.45.34: Then the monkey, whose prowess had the swiftness of the wind, drew near to him as he roamed the sky frequented by the king of birds, the wind and the Siddhas, and step by step seized him firmly by the feet.
t.5.45.35: That monkey, best of vānaras, whose valour equalled his father's, seized him as the lord of birds seizes a great serpent, whirled him around a thousand times, and in the battle hurled him with force onto the surface of the earth.
t.5.45.36: With his arms, thighs, hips and neck broken, streaming blood, his bones and eyes crushed, his joints shattered and his sinews scattered, that rākṣasa was struck dead upon the ground by the son of Vāyu.
t.5.45.37: Having crushed him upon the surface of the earth, the great monkey caused great fear to the lord of the Rākṣasas.
t.5.45.38: When the prince had been slain, that monkey was gazed upon by the great sages who move in the heavenly sphere and observe great vows, by the beings who had gathered together along with the Yakṣas and Pannagas, and by the gods together with Indra, all filled with great astonishment.
t.5.45.39: Having slain Prince Akṣa, whose splendour equalled that of the son of the Vajra-wielder and whose eyes were red as blood, the hero returned to that same archway, biding his moment like Kāla at the destruction of all creatures.
